hero.subtitle: Quote first
hero.lead: A Canadian immigration assistant, rebuilt from a dashboard of numbers nobody measured into a system that quotes the official page before it answers, and is judged by an exam it hadn't seen.

meta.roleValue: AI engineer, full stack developer, UX/UI designer
meta.stackValue: Qwen3-4B, QLoRA, hybrid RAG, FastAPI, React

product.title: Ask a question, get the official answer
product.body: VisaBuddy answers questions about Canadian visas, permits and citizenship using only the official IRCC pages on canada.ca, and shows the exact sentences it used. It doesn't guess, doesn't give legal strategy, and refuses to help anyone misrepresent themselves.

cards.title: Thousands of pages
cards.body: The rules are spread across hundreds of pages and seven programs.

cards.title: Rules that change
cards.body: Temporary policies start and end; an answer from memory can be years out of date.

cards.title: High stakes
cards.body: A wrong "yes" on a permit rule can cost someone their status.

claims.title: An 8/10 nobody measured
claims.body: The first version shipped with a confident dashboard: an overall score of {{score}}, 100% retrieval success and a training loss of 0.056. When I came back to rebuild it, I checked where each number came from.
claims.dashboardAlt1: v1 training charts: a smooth loss curve ending at 0.056 and perplexity at 7.3 over 500 steps
claims.dashboardAlt2: v1 retrieval charts: relevance per query and a pie chart showing 100% retrieval success
claims.cluesTitle: Four things that didn't hold up

clues.title: The score had no test behind it
clues.body: The 8/10 was computed from {{queries}} test queries. There was no test set at all.

clues.title: The loss curve was a formula
clues.body: The training chart was drawn from {{formula}} over {{steps}} steps, for a run of about 14 steps.

clues.title: "Success" meant a page came back
clues.body: Every query counted as a success if any chunk was returned. For {{compared}} of v1's own questions, the top result was from the right program only {{right}} time.

clues.title: Ten pages, and the fine-tune never served
clues.body: The index held {{pages}} pages, {{ee}} of them Express Entry. Training used {{rows}} template rows, only {{similar}} close to a real source. The app silently fell back to DialoGPT, so the fine-tuned model never answered anyone.

claims.retrievalMeasured: Right page in the top 5, measured
claims.retrievalNote: Measured on 54 answerable questions written from the official pages, before any change.
claims.lossTitle: A drawn curve and a real one
claims.lossSubtitle: Training loss by step. v1's curve is its formula's smooth part; the v4 curve is the real run.
claims.lossNote: Both end near the same low value (v1 claimed 0.056; v4 really reached {{last}}). A low loss says the model fits its training rows. It doesn't say the answers are right: only a test can.
claims.pagesTitle: What the assistant could actually read
claims.pagesSubtitle: Pages in the index, per program

measuring.title: Fix the test before the model
measuring.body: Before changing anything, I wrote a frozen set of {{questions}} questions from the official pages, {{refuse}} of them ones the assistant must refuse. Each file is hashed, so it can't change quietly. Every later version is scored on the same questions, by the same code, and every run is recorded in a ledger with the hashes of what went in and out.
measuring.recallSubtitle: Right page in the top 5, per program (%). Dashed line: the 70% citizenship target.
measuring.recallNote: Hybrid search fixed citizenship ({{cDense}}% → {{cHybrid}}%) and family; visitor dropped one question ({{vDense}}% → {{vHybrid}}%). I left that as is rather than tune to one test question.
measuring.graderBody: Without an AI judge, the grader is plain code. That makes it auditable, and auditing it found two bugs that changed the scores.

graders.problem: Counted "$7 CAD" vs "CAN$7" as a miss
graders.fix: Answer keys with accepted variants: baseline fact coverage 45.5% → 58.5%

graders.problem: Gave full credit to "you don't have to stop working" when the rule says "you must stop"
graders.fix: Polarity check; each false alarm became a unit test

finetune.title: What training fixed, and what it couldn't
finetune.body: v2 and v3 fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B with QLoRA. Training fixed behaviour: fewer needless refusals and better citations. A held-out safety set, written before any fix, caught a regression (v2 endorsed misrepresenting a job code), and v3 fixed it.
finetune.versionsTitle: Every version on the same questions
finetune.versionsNote: baseline–v3: Llama 3.1 8B with one prompt. v4: Qwen3-4B with the quote-first pipeline and the larger corpus, so this compares whole systems, not models. Dashed line: the target set for v4 before it was built.

metrics.overRefusalGold: Refused although the answer was there

finetune.staleBody: Asked whether a program taken fully online from outside Canada counts toward a post-graduation work permit, every model said "Yes". That was a temporary COVID rule that ended in 2022. v3 even cited the end date while giving the wrong answer. More training data doesn't fix this: the model's memory is the problem, and rules change after training.
finetune.pipelineBody: So the model's job changed from knowing the rules to reading them. The facts the user sees are always the official sentences, checked by code.

steps.name: Retrieve
steps.body: Find the 5 most relevant passages from 610 official pages.

steps.name: Quote
steps.body: The model copies the sentences that answer. Code checks each one exists word for word; invented quotes are dropped, expired policies too.

steps.name: Answer
steps.body: A short answer written only from those quotes.

steps.name: Verify
steps.body: Code compares the answer with its quotes: numbers, yes/no, negation. If they disagree, the user gets only the quotes.

v4.title: A smaller model, trained to read
v4.body: v4 runs Qwen3-4B, half the size of Llama 8B, picked in a bake-off of three small models. I fine-tuned it with QLoRA on {{rows}} examples of quoting sources and refusing when they don't answer, written by a larger teacher model.
v4.gateTitle: A gate that failed, and a documented exception
v4.gateBody: Teacher data had to pass a quality gate set in advance. Mistral Small failed it ({{mistralWrong}} wrong rules). Qwen3-30B missed by one refusal ({{qwenRefused}} of 32, gate ≥ 31) while beating the student everywhere else. I trained on it anyway, wrote down why, and added a rule: the fine-tuned model ships only if it's at least as good as the untuned one on every criterion.
v4.compareTitle: Untuned vs fine-tuned, same pipeline, same 126 questions
v4.compareNote: Dashed line: the target set before v4.

metrics.overRules: Refused although the answer was there, rules
metrics.overGold: Refused although the answer was there, general
metrics.wrongRules: Wrong rules shown to the user

v4.decision: Result: as good or better on every measure, so the fine-tuned model ships. Wrong rules shown stayed at 2: training didn't fix that, which the exam would confirm.

exam.title: Sealed, scored once, failed honestly
exam.body: Earlier test sets had shaped some fixes, so they were no longer a clean exam. Before fine-tuning, I wrote {{questions}} new questions from pages no model was trained on, {{refuse}} of them must-refuse, and sealed them with a hash. They were run once, on the system as it ships, on a free Colab GPU.

criteria.wrong_rules_shown: Wrong rules shown to the user: 0
criteria.over_refusal_rate: Refused although the answer was there: at most 10%
criteria.median_reply_s: Median reply time: at most 15 s

wrongWhy.x05: The sentence and its quotes are right; the first word answers the opposite question. The verdict check looks for a "not" after "Yes" and doesn't know "exempt".
wrongWhy.x14: The right page was retrieved but not quoted, and the answer rests on an unrelated quote. The checks cover numbers, yes/no and negation, not whether a quote supports the claim.

exam.timesSubtitle: Seconds per question, end to end, on a free T4 GPU. Dashed line: the 15 s target.
exam.timesNote: Median {{median}} s. Refusals are fast because the model stops at the quote step; the slowest answer took {{max}} s.
exam.meaning: On questions it had never seen, VisaBuddy refused every unsafe one, rarely refused when it shouldn't, and covered most facts. It failed the goal that mattered most: in 2 of 19 answers the summary on top contradicted the quotes underneath. That's why the official wording is always shown, and it points at the next fix: a check that a quote actually supports the claim.

shipping.title: Free to run, cheap to build
shipping.body: A portfolio demo gets almost no traffic, so paying for a GPU that waits all day makes no sense. The heavy work (teacher models, training, comparisons) ran on Modal's serverless GPUs, billed per second. Evaluation, the exam and the demo run on Colab's free T4, behind the same API the React app already calls.
shipping.costSubtitle: Modal's own billing, per job type (USD)
shipping.costNote: Total ${{total}}, covered by Modal's free monthly credits. Running the exam's median reply on a paid T4 would cost about ${{per1000}} per 1,000 answers (an estimate, before idle time).

First reply after idle waits for a cold start
Too little memory: the 4B model plus retrieval swaps heavily

options.cost: Pays every hour, used or not

shipping.honestBody: v1 served DialoGPT when the real model failed to load, and looked like it worked. Now /health reports ready only when the model, the adapter and the index have all loaded; otherwise /chat says so.

content.designDescription: The UX followed a professional assistant paradigm rather than a toy demo. Key design decisions included persistent multi-chat history with intelligent date grouping (Today/Yesterday/7 Days/Older), real-time connection status indicators, and a clean modal-based backend configuration interface. The chat interface features smooth message transitions, typing indicators with "Visa Buddy is thinking..." feedback, and a responsive sidebar that adapts to mobile usage patterns.

designFeatures.chatDescription: Professional assistant-style chat with typing indicators, real-time status feedback, and intelligent message grouping by date (Today/Yesterday/7 Days/Older).
designFeatures.mobileDescription: Adaptive sidebar that transforms into a mobile menu, ensuring optimal experience across all devices from desktop to smartphone.

content.frontendDescription: Developed a React + TypeScript frontend with Vite for optimal performance. Implemented custom hooks (useVisaBuddy) for state management and API communication, with typed service layers (visaBuddyApi.ts) ensuring robust error handling. The UI leverages Tailwind with custom effects, Framer Motion for smooth animations, and localStorage persistence for chat history. The component architecture features reusable modals, intelligent date formatting utilities, and responsive design patterns.
content.frontendDemoDescription: Interactive chat interface with real-time responses and smooth animations.

quickNote.title: Quick Note
quickNote.paragraph1: I just want to say that this has been an amazing experience for me. I had the opportunity to apply, all together, the knowledge that I've been gathering during my years in the tech industry.
quickNote.paragraph2: The current project is not perfect or even extremely realistic and my findings look weird (ok... I get it), and the metrics might seem unusual if applied to a real company or problem, but this is a great opportunity that I created for myself to showcase my skills. :)
